chunks: And Muhammad ibn al-Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fudalah, from Ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): like it.
And he added and said: 'On the Day of Arafah, they gather without an Imam in the cities, supplicating to Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty.'

And from him, from al-Hasan, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about the man who does not go out on the Day of al-Fitr and al-Adha, is there a prayer for him alone? He said: 'Yes.'

And from him, from Umar ibn Ja'far, who said: Abd Allah ibn Muhammad narrated to us from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, from Mansur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: 'My father was ill on the Day of al-Adha, so he prayed two rak'ahs in his house, then offered the sacrifice.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for Eid prayer if one cannot attend the congregation?
ai.summary: These narrations from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarify the flexibility of Eid prayer jurisprudence, affirming that individual performance at home is valid for those unable to attend the congregation, as demonstrated by Imam al-Sadiq (AS) praying two rak'ahs while ill. The texts further highlight the communal spirit of supplication on the Day of Arafah, noting that gatherings in cities often occur without a formal Imam, emphasizing the accessibility of divine connection during these sacred times.
